prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The week in August you come home, adult, professional, aloof, we roast and carve the fatted calf —in our case home-grown pig, the chine garlicked and crisped, the applesauce hand-pressed. Hand-pressed the greengage wine. Nothing is cost-effective here. The peas, the beets, the lettuces hand sown, are raised to stand apart. The electric fence ticks like the slow heart of something we fed and bedded for a year, then killed with kindness’s one bullet and paid Jake Mott to do the butchering. In winter we lure the birds with suet, thaw lungs and kidneys for the cat. Darlings, it’s all a circle from the ring of wire that keeps the raccoons from the corn to the gouged pine table that we lounge around, distressed before any of you was born. Benign and dozy from our gluttonies, the candles down to stubs, defenses down, love leaking out unguarded the way juice dribbles from the fence when grounded by grass stalks or a forgotten hoe, how eloquent, how beautiful you seem! Wearing our gestures, how wise you grow, ballooning to overfill our space, the almost-parents of your parents now. So briefly having you back to measure us is harder than having let you go.

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version of your text, refined for greater eloquence while preserving its imagery, structure, and emotional depth:

---

That week in August when you come home—adult now, professional, faintly distant—we roast and carve the fatted calf, though here it is our own home-raised pig, its chine garlicked and crisped to gold, the applesauce hand-pressed, the greengage wine hand-pressed as well. Nothing here is measured by efficiency. The peas, the beets, the lettuces, all hand-sown, are raised to stand apart from what the world provides. The electric fence hums like the slow heartbeat of something we fed and sheltered for a year, then dispatched with the single mercy of a bullet, leaving the butchering to Jake Mott's practiced hand. Come winter, we tempt the birds with suet, and thaw lungs and kidneys for the cat.

Darlings, it is all a circle—from the ring of wire that keeps the raccoons from the corn, to the gouged pine table around which we lounge, its wood already worn before any of you were born. Sated and drowsy from our indulgences, the candles burned to stubs, our guards let down, love seeps out unguarded, the way current leaks from the fence when grounded by a blade of grass or a forgotten hoe—how eloquent, how lovely you seem in that light! Wearing our old gestures, you grow wiser still, expanding to fill our space entirely, becoming, in some strange way, the almost-parents of your parents now. To have you back so briefly, only to take our measure, proves harder than the letting go ever was.

---

I preserved the central metaphors (the fatted calf, the electric fence, the circle of life) and all specific details (Jake Mott, greengage wine, suet) while smoothing transitions, refining word choice for a more formal register, and enhancing the rhythmic flow of the prose-poem. Let me know if you'd like a version with a different tone—more spare, more lyrical, or more conversational—and I can adjust accordingly.

That August week you return—grown now, businesslike, a little distant—we prepare the celebration meal, slaughtering our own pig instead of the biblical calf. The back cut wears its garlic crust, and the applesauce beside it was pressed by our own hands, just like the greengage wine. Nothing here follows an economical logic. Even the peas and beets and lettuce heads were sown by hand, cultivated to become something exceptional. That electric wire hums steadily, echoing the pulse of a creature we raised and sheltered through the seasons before ending its life as gently as violence allows, leaving the actual butchering to Jake Mott's expertise.

Come winter, suet draws songbirds to us, while organ meats thaw for the cat's dinner. My dears, everything connects—the wire that guards the corn from raccoon raids, the worn old pine table where we gather, already weathered before any of you existed. Loosened by our own excess, watching candles burn low, our guard drops and affection spills freely, like current escaping the fence when grass or an abandoned tool touches ground—and in that unguarded moment, how striking, how lovely you appear!

Carrying traces of us in your movements, you seem to grow more knowing, filling up the space we occupy until you become something like guardians to those who raised you. This fleeting visit, this brief chance to size up who we've become, proves harder to bear than the original letting go ever was.
outputs.L3:
# A Homecoming Feast: The Bittersweet Harvest of Family Love

When their adult child returns home for a week in August, the family marks the occasion with a feast unlike any ordinary meal—one steeped in labor, memory, and quiet devotion. Roast pig glistens at the center of the table, flanked by applesauce pressed by hand and wine crafted from grapes tended through countless seasons. This is not merely food; it is an offering, a physical manifestation of months and years of care poured into the soil and into the animals that will nourish the family once more.

Nothing on this farm exists for the sake of efficiency. The vegetables were not chosen for their yield-per-acre or their resistance to pests, but were planted, weeded, and harvested because someone wanted to watch them grow. The livestock, too, defies any economic logic—raised not as commodities but as creatures deserving of attention, patience, and even affection. In a world increasingly governed by convenience and cost-effectiveness, this family's way of living stands as a quiet rebellion, a testament to the belief that some things are worth doing simply because they matter, not because they make sense on a balance sheet.

The pig, the centerpiece of the feast, embodies this philosophy most poignantly. It was raised with kindness, fed with a steady hand, and ultimately killed—not out of cruelty, but as part of an unavoidable cycle that the family has come to accept, even honor. This tension between nurture and loss threads through everything: the care given to a living creature does not exempt it from its eventual end, but perhaps that care is what gives the ending its meaning. The poem seems to suggest that love does not negate mortality—it simply makes the passage through it more bearable, more human.

As the meal progresses and the wine flows, the parents find themselves softened, their usual vigilance dissolving into something more tender and unguarded. The food and drink loosen not just their bodies but their emotional defenses, allowing love to "leak out" without restraint. In this state of openness, their children appear transformed before their eyes—more articulate, more radiant, more fully realized than perhaps they truly are. It is as though the parents are seeing their children not as they exist in daily life, but as they exist in memory and hope: eloquent, beautiful, whole.

Yet this same clarity brings with it an unexpected ache. The children who have returned are no longer children in any meaningful sense—they have grown into adults so capable, so assured, that they seem to have become something like "almost-parents of your parents." The natural hierarchy has quietly shifted; the ones who were once nurtured now radiate a maturity that makes the older generation feel, if only briefly, cared for in return. 

This inversion, however welcome, carries its own sorrow. The parents realize, perhaps for the first time, that having their children back—even for a short, joyous week—is somehow more difficult than the original act of letting them go. The letting go was gradual, expected, softened by the slow unfolding of time. But this return, however brief and however loving, forces the parents to confront how much has changed, how much has been missed, and how fleeting even this reunion will be. In the end, the feast becomes not just a celebration of homecoming, but a meditation on impermanence—on how love, labor, and loss are always intertwined, and how the sweetest reunions carry within them the seeds of the next departure.
outputs.L4:
**Homecoming, Late August**

They come home when the corn stands shoulder-high,
when the pig has been fattened all summer on scraps
and windfall apples, and my father wakes before light
to build the fire pit, laying oak and hickory
in a crosshatch he learned from his own father,
who learned it from a man whose name we've lost.

By noon the yard smells of smoke and sweetgrass.
My mother moves between the kitchen and the porch,
her hands finding the rhythm of forty Augusts—
snap beans into the blue bowl, corn silk drifting
like the hair we used to pull from her collar
when we were small enough to be carried.

The children who are children no longer arrive
in cars that cost more than the land they're standing on,
and for a moment there is only noise: screen door,
gravel, the dog's arthritic joy. Then the quiet
underneath it, the way a held breath sits
beneath a laugh.

We press the grapes for wine the way we always have,
feet purple in the barrel, though our feet are older now,
softer in places, and my brother's daughter watches
from the fence line where the electric wire hums
its low warning—*don't touch, don't touch*—
a lesson none of us needed twice.

At the table, someone reaches to cut my father's meat
before he asks. Someone notices my mother's hand
trembling around the pitcher and takes it, gently,
the way you'd take something from a child
learning not to spill. We do not speak of this.
We pass the plates. We talk about the weather,
the price of feed, the fence that needs repairing
before the frost.

But I am watching my mother watch her son
tend the fire she used to tend alone,
and I understand, finally, what no one tells you—
that raising children who then have to raise you
is a grief with no name, arriving late,
disguised as love, as help, as *let me get that*.

The pig turns slowly on its spit. The wine
will not be ready for a year. We eat
until the light goes copper, then blue,
then dark enough to see the first few stars
appear like something earned. Someone laughs
too loudly. Someone cries without explaining why.

Tomorrow they will leave again, and this time
it will not feel like the day I dropped them
at some dormitory door, my chest a fist,
watching them walk without turning back.
This time, I will stand at the end of the drive
long after the taillights blur to nothing,
and understand that letting go the first time
was only practice—

that the real leaving happens now,
in this brief return, this feast, this fire
we built together and will bank down separately,
each of us carrying embers back
to our own small, quiet houses,
where the ash keeps warm for days.
outputs.L5:
# The August Hand

The August heat hung heavy over the valley, and it was in this stillness that old Marcus first noticed his hand had begun to shake. Not violently—just a faint tremor, like a leaf catching an almost imperceptible breeze. He sat on his porch, watching the golden light filter through the trees, and studied his own fingers as if they belonged to someone else.

He had worked with these hands for sixty years. They had planted seeds, mended fences, held his children when they were small, and later, held his wife's hand as she slipped away one winter morning. Now, in the thick August air, they trembled with a message he didn't want to hear.

Marcus flexed his fingers slowly, watching the tendons rise beneath weathered skin. The hand that had once swung a hammer with confidence, that had shaped wood into furniture people still used decades later, now struggled to hold a coffee cup steady.

He thought about time—how it moves like August itself, languid and thick, until suddenly you realize the season is ending. The tomatoes in his garden were ripening fast now, racing against the calendar. Soon the first cool nights would arrive, and everything would change.

But for now, he had this moment: the porch, the heat, and his own hand resting on the armrest, still capable, still his, even as it whispered of autumns yet to come. He pressed it flat against the wood and felt the day's warmth radiating back, a small comfort against the passage of time.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about a grown child returning home for a visit, told from the parent's point of view, using rich imagery of a home-grown farm dinner.
counterfactuals.output:
# Setting the Table for You

I peeled the potatoes the way you like—
rough, with little moons of skin left clinging,
because you once said perfect felt like nothing to hold onto.

The tomatoes came in warm from the vine an hour ago,
still wearing the sun on their shoulders,
and I sliced them thick as the summers
you spent barefoot in that dirt,
knees green, hands full of small discoveries.

Corn boils on the back burner.
I grew it tall this year, taller than you were
the last time you stood in that doorway
with everything you owned in two duffel bags
and a future I couldn't see the edges of.

The beans I snapped by hand this morning,
sitting on the porch step, listening
for tires on gravel,
for a sound I've memorized
in every season since you learned to drive.

I set two glasses of the sweet tea you loved at sixteen,
though I know your tastes have widened since—
you'll ask about the coffee now, the wine,
some restaurant in the city I can't pronounce.
I keep the tea anyway. Some rooms
in a mother's house don't get remodeled.

The bread is rising in the window light,
dough breathing like something alive,
and it is—
it is the same yeast, the same flour,
the same hands shaping what will hold us.

When you walk through that door
smelling like the world,
carrying opinions I didn't teach you
and a laugh that still turns
into the child who used to fall asleep
against my shoulder at the dinner table,

I will not ask where you've been.

I will only say: *sit down, sit down,*
*the tomatoes are still warm,*
*let me fill your plate*
*the way I filled your hands once,*
*the way I'm still trying to fill this house*
*with everything I planted so it would still be here*
*when you came home.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem that reimagines the "prodigal son" homecoming through details of butchering a pig, canning, and rural self-sufficiency, ending on a bittersweet note about roles reversing between parent and child.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Fatted Pig

They didn't kill a calf when I came home—
we don't keep cattle, never could afford it.
Dad had already scalded water in the drum,
already sharpened every blade he owned.

I found him at the sawhorse, arms bright red
to the elbow, the pig hung open like a door
swung wide on something private. He looked up
the way you'd greet a stranger, then he didn't.

*Good,* he said. *You're here for the scraping.*

So this was homecoming: not a robe, not rings,
but rubber gloves two sizes far too small,
the bristles coming off in fistfuls, steam
still rising off the flesh like it remembered
being warm, being alive, being anything
but supper.

We worked in that particular quiet
of people who've said everything already
in the years apart, or never learned the words.
He showed me how to find the seam of fat,
how not to nick the bladder, how the liver
comes out easy if you're patient with the knife.
I hadn't held a blade like that in years.
My hands remembered anyway.

Mom was inside, boiling jars for hours,
lids popping their small applause
as each one sealed—pickled feet, head cheese,
the fat rendered down to lard so white
it looked like something holy, something saved.
Nothing wasted. Nothing thrown away.
That was the lesson, though nobody preached it:
you use the whole animal or you don't deserve it.

That night we ate the tenderloin, the best part,
because apparently I still rated that,
still counted as somebody worth the good cut
even after everything, even after leaving
like the leaving was an insult to the land itself.

*I'm sorry,* I said, finally, over the plates.

*For what,* Dad said. *You came back for the pig-killing.
That's not nothing. That's not sorry-shaped at all.*

I noticed then the way his hands had started
to shake a little, holding his fork,
the way he'd asked me twice to pass the salt
though it sat right there in front of him.

I noticed how the barn looked smaller,
how the porch step had that give in it
that means the wood's about to fail,
how he'd needed me to finish jointing the shoulder,
how he'd needed me at all.

Somewhere in the making of it—
the canning, the salting, the long slow smoke
that would cure into winter—
we had traded chairs at the table
without either of us standing up.

Next fall, I understood, I'd be the one
sharpening the knives at dawn,
scalding water in the drum,
waiting to see if he came home to help,
already knowing in my gut, the way you know
a storm before the sky admits it,
that this was the last one we'd do together,
that I'd have to learn to render fat alone,
that the whole animal doesn't keep forever,
that neither, now, do we.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary poem about hosting an adult child home from the city, blending sensory descriptions of food (roast pork, applesauce, wine) with reflections on aging and letting go.
counterfactuals.output:
# Sunday, Late September

The pork shoulder's been turning since dawn,
skin blistering to amber, fat singing
its slow confession into the pan—
I baste it like a prayer I've said so many times
the words have worn smooth as river stone.

You arrive smelling of trains and someone else's city,
your coat still cold from a world I only visit
through the phone's small window. I take it anyway,
hang it where your child-sized jackets used to hang,
and for a moment the hook holds both of you.

The applesauce is simple—just Macouns
breaking down to gold, a cinnamon stick
stirring itself to sleep. I make it too sweet.
I always make it too sweet. You'll say nothing,
eat two bowls, and this is how we speak now:
in portions, in seconds, in what gets finished.

The wine breathes on the counter, something red
I chose because you liked it once, at twenty-three,
in a different kitchen, before you knew
what leaving cost, before I knew
that raising you was mostly a rehearsal
for this—the pouring out, the letting steep.

At the table, you tell me about the city:
its noise, its promise, its particular loneliness
you wear like a coat you're still deciding on.
I listen and carve the meat too thin,
my hands remembering when they held you whole,
now merely passing plates, refilling glass,
practicing the smaller gestures of a life
that's learning how to love you from a distance.

Outside, the maple's already turning,
that violent orange that means the year
is doing what years do—not ending,
just becoming something else. I think:
this is the lesson wine and roasting teach,
the one applesauce knows in its slow collapse—
that tenderness requires a kind of ruin,
that what we make must eventually be eaten,
that setting down the fork, at last, is also
a way of saying: *yes. Go back.
I have fed you. I can let you go again.*

The bottle empties slower than I'd like.
Outside, your coat waits by the door,
already gathering the cold
it will carry you back into.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem in second person addressing a visiting adult child, weaving together farm chores, an electric fence, and the emotional charge of a family reunion.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Visit

You pull into the gravel drive at noon,
dust announcing you before you speak,
and your father is already at the fence line,
pliers in his back pocket, waiting
like he's been standing there since March.

You change your clothes without being asked.
The boots by the door still fit,
though your feet have walked away
from this place a thousand times.

Together you walk the perimeter,
checking for breaks, for sag,
for the places where the wire
has grown tired of holding a current.
He touches it first, always,
the back of his hand testing
what the years have taught him
to trust before he lets you near it.

*It's live,* he says. *Feel it.*

And you do — that quick bright jolt
that says *stay awake, stay in the field,
this is what keeps the herd together* —
and you laugh, the way you did at eleven,
shaking out your hand,
your mother calling from the porch
that supper's in an hour, wash up.

This is how you love each other:
not in words but in fence posts,
in the mineral tubs you fill together,
in the silences between the barn and house
where everything unsaid
still manages to get said.

At dinner, your sister brings up
things from years ago — small hurts
still carrying their charge,
still able to snap you back
if you get too close, too careless.
Your mother changes the subject
the way she's always changed the subject,
passing the potatoes like a peace offering.

Tomorrow you'll leave before light,
your father's hand raised from the porch,
not quite a wave, more like a man
checking to see if it's still raining,
if the current's still running
through everything he built
to keep you close
without ever holding on too hard.

Drive safe, he'll say.
And you will feel it all the way home —
that hum in the wire,
that reminder: *this fence
is what love looks like
when it has to reach so far.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a nostalgic, image-heavy poem about parents preparing an elaborate homemade feast for their grown child's brief visit, exploring themes of pride, labor, and the ache of impermanent closeness.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Table Set for One Weekend

My mother has been cooking since Tuesday,
though I don't arrive until Friday night—
the freezer bags stacked like sedimentary rock,
each one dated in her careful hand:
*dumplings, 11/12. sauce, 11/13.*

She is building a geological record
of how long she has missed me.

In the kitchen, my father stands guard
over a pot that doesn't need guarding,
stirring nothing into something,
something into more,
his reading glasses fogged with steam,
a dish towel over his shoulder
like a soldier's flag, unearned rank
he wears anyway because someone
has to hold the door
between the stove and the waiting.

They have not slept properly in days.
I know this because the roast
takes eleven hours, and my mother
does not trust the timer,
sits up watching the oven light
like it might blink out, might
take the whole house with it—
her vigilance a kind of prayer
she doesn't call prayer.

By the time I walk in, the table
is a small country I don't recognize:
five kinds of pickled things,
the good bowls out, the ones
with the chip turned toward the wall
so I won't see it, won't worry,
won't say *let's just use paper plates, it's fine.*

It is never fine. It is everything.

They have made enough food
for a family reunion, a wedding,
a wake—
enough to prove that love,
if measured correctly,
weighs exactly as much
as three days' worth of chopping,
the onions that made my mother cry
before I'd said a single word
to make her.

I eat until I can't.
I eat like I am storing it
for the drought of my own kitchen,
three states away, where I will microwave
things that taste like nothing,
where no one waits up
to hear my car in the driveway.

Sunday comes too fast,
the way it always does,
the way the whole visit
was just a held breath
between goodbyes.

My mother packs leftovers
into more bags, more dates,
already grieving the meal
before I've even left the table,
already planning the next one
though she says nothing of it,
just presses containers into my hands
like she's trying to send
her whole self home with me,
sealed in Tupperware,
labeled so I won't forget
how long, how long,
how long she'll wait
for the sound of my car again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
